**The Museum of Almosts**

If you give me a thousand words, I won't spend them all at once. I'll keep a few in my pocket for later — for someone crying quietly on a train who doesn't know why, for a morning when the kettle takes too long and everything feels unbearably ordinary and needs rescuing. Words spoil if you hoard them, but they also disappear if you scatter them too carelessly. So I'll spend these carefully, on this:

There is, in my mind, a museum that doesn't exist. It's not grand. It's a small, drafty building at the end of a street that most maps forget to finish. No marble steps, no gift shop. Just a hand-painted sign above the door: THE MUSEUM OF ALMOSTS. Admission is free, but you have to leave something behind when you go.

Inside are the things people nearly did.

In the first room are the unsent letters. Thousands of them, folded into envelopes that were licked and then, at the last second, not sealed. Apologies written at 2 a.m. Confessions practiced in handwriting to make them feel braver. A letter from a father to a son that begins, "I don't know how to say this out loud, so —" and then stops, as if even paper was too loud. They are arranged not by date, but by weight. Some are so heavy the shelves bow.

The second room is quieter. It holds the almost-spoken sentences. You can hear them if you stand still enough. *I love you* said to a closing elevator door. *Stay* swallowed at an airport. *That hurt me* turned, mid-breath, into *never mind, I'm fine.* The curator has put little benches in this room because people tend to need to sit down in it. I imagine she knows why.

The curator's name is Mara. She is not young and not old in the way that matters. She wears sweaters with pockets full of pencils and string and other people's lost buttons. She took the job because she has a good memory for things other people are trying to forget, and she thought that should be useful somewhere. Every evening she walks the halls with a duster she rarely uses. Dust, she says, is just proof that something stayed.

People bring her things during the day. A woman brings the wedding vows she wrote for a marriage that lasted eleven months; she doesn't want to throw them away because the words were true, even if the promise wasn't. A teenage boy brings a song he almost sang at the school concert before panic closed his throat. He hums it for Mara, once, very quietly, and she writes down the title and files the silence where the performance would have been. An old man brings nothing in his hands at all. "I almost told my brother I forgave him," he says. "He died last spring." Mara nods and makes room on a shelf anyway. Empty space, catalogued and labeled, is still a kind of holding.

My favorite room is at the back, where the light is best. It's the Room of Almost-Begun Lives. A pair of ballet shoes, never scuffed. A passport with one stamp. A business card for a bakery that never opened, its name still hopeful in gold lettering: *Second Rise.* A train ticket to a city where someone was going to become an entirely different person — braver, kinder, less tired. Mara doesn't arrange these things sadly. She puts them near the windows. "Almost," she likes to say, "is not the same as never. Almost means you aimed your life at something. That counts for weather in the soul."

Once, a visitor asked her if the museum was depressing. She laughed, surprised. "Oh, no," she said. "You should see what people take with them when they leave." Because that's the secret rule of the place: you must leave something behind, but you may also take something out. Not the objects — those stay. You take permission. People leave carrying it strangely, like a coat they've never worn before. Permission to send a different letter. To say the sentence badly and late rather than perfectly and never. To begin at fifty, at seventy, with shaking hands.

I think about this museum more than I should, especially at night, when my own almosts line up politely beside the bed. The friendships I let go quiet. The version of myself who learned the piano, who called more often, who wasn't so afraid of being a beginner in public. They don't accuse me, exactly. They just wait, like exhibits, to see if I'll visit.

So if I have words to spend, I'll spend the last of them on this small instruction, the one Mara writes on a card by the exit, in pencil, in case it needs changing:

*Take one almost with you. Not the heaviest one. The one that still warms when you touch it. Carry it out into the ordinary street. See what it becomes in the daylight.*

The rest of the words can stay in my pocket. Someone will need them later.
